name: Circle area (πr²)
description: Calculates the area of a circle from its radius r by multiplying pi (about 3.14159) by the radius squared. Doubling the radius quadruples the area, because it grows with the square of the radius.
notes: r is the radius, not the diameter. From a diameter d, use pi×(d/2)². Keep length and area units consistent (a radius in cm gives an area in cm²).

name: Circle circumference (2πr)
description: Computes the circumference (perimeter) of a circle from its radius r, using 2×pi×r. The result is the distance once around the circle in the same length unit as the radius.
notes: Input the radius, not the diameter; if you have the diameter, halve it first. The output length uses the same unit as r.

name: Triangle area
description: Calculates the area of a triangle as base×height÷2. Height must be the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite vertex, not the length of a slanted side.
notes: Base and height must be in the same length unit; the area comes out in that unit squared. Use the perpendicular height, not a slant side length.

name: Sphere volume
description: Computes the volume of a sphere from its radius r using (4/3)×pi×r³. The result is the space enclosed by the sphere in the cube of the radius unit.
notes: Enter the radius, not the diameter. Because the radius is cubed, small radius errors are amplified strongly in the result.

name: Pythagorean (hypotenuse)
description: Finds the hypotenuse of a right triangle from its two perpendicular sides a and b, using √(a²+b²). The result is the length of the side opposite the right angle.
notes: Valid only for right triangles; a and b must be the two legs meeting at the 90° corner, in the same length unit.

name: Rectangle area
description: Calculates the area of a rectangle by multiplying its width w by its height h. The result is in squared units of whatever length unit is used for the two sides.
notes: Width and height must be in the same unit; the result is that unit squared. Applies only to true rectangles with right angles, not to general parallelograms.

name: Square area
description: Gives the area of a square by squaring its side length a. The result is in squared units of the side length.
notes: All four sides are assumed equal. The result unit is the side unit squared.

name: Parallelogram area
description: Calculates the area of a parallelogram by multiplying its base b by its perpendicular height h. The result is in squared units of the length unit used.
notes: The height h must be the perpendicular distance between the two parallel bases, not the length of the slanted side.

name: Trapezoid area
description: Computes the area of a trapezoid by averaging its two parallel bases a and b and multiplying by the height h. The result is in squared units of the length unit used.
notes: The two bases a and b must be the parallel sides, and h must be the perpendicular distance between them, not a slanted side.

name: Rhombus area (diagonals)
description: Gives the area of a rhombus as half the product of its two diagonals d1 and d2. The result is in squared units of the length unit used.
notes: Requires the diagonals, which in a rhombus cross at right angles, not the side length. The same half-product-of-diagonals rule works for any quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals.

name: Kite area (diagonals)
description: Calculates the area of a kite as half the product of its two diagonals p and q. The result is in squared units of the length unit used.
notes: In a kite the diagonals are perpendicular, which is why the half-product rule applies. Provide the full diagonal lengths, not half-diagonals.

name: Heron's formula (triangle area)
description: Computes the area of a triangle from its three side lengths a, b and c using Heron's formula, which forms the semiperimeter s = (a+b+c)/2 and takes the square root of s times (s-a)(s-b)(s-c). The result is in squared length units.
notes: The three sides must satisfy the triangle inequality (each side less than the sum of the other two), otherwise the value under the root is negative and no real triangle exists.

name: Equilateral triangle area
description: Gives the area of an equilateral triangle from its side length a, equal to the square root of three over four times a squared. The result is in squared units of the side length.
notes: Valid only when all three sides are equal. For a general triangle use Heron's formula or base times height instead.

name: Regular polygon area
description: Calculates the area of a regular polygon with n equal sides of length s, as n times s squared divided by four times the tangent of pi over n. The result is in squared units of the side length.
notes: Applies only to regular (equal-sided, equal-angled) polygons and requires n to be at least 3. The angle pi/n is in radians, as the tangent function here expects.

name: Ellipse area
description: Computes the area of an ellipse as pi times its semi-major axis a times its semi-minor axis b. When a equals b this reduces to the area of a circle of that radius. The result is in squared length units.
notes: Use the semi-axes (half the full axis lengths), not the full diameters. Unlike its area, the perimeter of an ellipse has no simple closed form.

name: Circular sector area
description: Gives the area of a circular sector (a pie-slice wedge) as half the radius r squared times the central angle theta. The result is in squared units of the radius.
notes: The central angle theta must be in radians. For a full circle use theta equal to 2 pi, which recovers pi r squared.

name: Arc length
description: Calculates the length of a circular arc as the radius r multiplied by the central angle theta. The result is a length in the same unit as the radius.
notes: The central angle theta must be in radians; this simple product does not hold for degrees. For a full turn use theta equal to 2 pi to recover the circumference.

name: Circular segment area
description: Computes the area of a circular segment, the region between a chord and its arc, as half the radius r squared times theta minus the sine of theta. The result is in squared units of the radius.
notes: The central angle theta must be in radians. It equals the sector area minus the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.

name: Annulus area (ring)
description: Gives the area of an annulus (a flat ring) as pi times the difference between the squared outer radius R and the squared inner radius r. The result is in squared units of the radii.
notes: The outer radius R must be larger than the inner radius r or the area is negative. Subtract the squares of the radii, not the radii themselves.

name: Sphere surface area
description: Calculates the surface area of a sphere as four times pi times the radius r squared. The result is in squared units of the radius.
notes: Uses the radius, not the diameter; halve the diameter first if that is what you have. This is exactly four times the area of a great circle of the same sphere.

name: Cylinder volume
description: Computes the volume of a right circular cylinder as pi times the radius r squared times the height h. It is the circular base area multiplied by the height. The result is in cubed units of the length unit used.
notes: Radius and height must share the same unit; the result is that unit cubed. Applies to a straight (right) cylinder with a uniform circular cross-section.

name: Cylinder surface area
description: Gives the total surface area of a closed right cylinder as two pi times the radius r times the sum of the radius and height (r plus h). This combines the two circular ends and the curved side. The result is in squared length units.
notes: This includes both end caps; for the curved side only, use the lateral surface formula. Radius and height must be in the same unit.

name: Cylinder lateral surface
description: Calculates only the curved side surface of a cylinder as two pi times the radius r times the height h, excluding the two circular ends. The result is in squared length units.
notes: This is the unrolled rectangle of width 2 pi r and height h; it does not include the top and bottom caps. Use the same unit for radius and height.

name: Cone volume
description: Computes the volume of a right circular cone as pi times the radius r squared times the height h, divided by three. It equals one third of the cylinder with the same base and height. The result is in cubed length units.
notes: The height h is the perpendicular (axial) height from base to apex, not the slant height. Radius and height must share the same unit.

name: Cone lateral surface
description: Gives the curved side surface area of a right circular cone as pi times the radius r times the slant height, where the slant height is the square root of r squared plus h squared. The result is in squared length units.
notes: This excludes the circular base. The input h is the perpendicular height; the formula computes the slant height internally, so do not supply the slant length directly.

name: Cone total surface area
description: Calculates the full surface area of a right circular cone as pi times the radius r times the sum of the radius and the slant height (square root of r squared plus h squared). This adds the base circle to the curved side. The result is in squared length units.
notes: The input h is the perpendicular height, not the slant height, which the formula derives. This total includes the base; omit it for the lateral surface only.

name: Cube volume
description: Gives the volume of a cube by cubing its edge length a. The result is in cubed units of the edge length.
notes: All twelve edges are assumed equal. The result unit is the edge unit cubed.

name: Cube surface area
description: Calculates the total surface area of a cube as six times its edge length a squared, since a cube has six identical square faces. The result is in squared units of the edge length.
notes: Assumes a perfect cube with all edges equal. The result unit is the edge unit squared.

name: Rectangular box volume
description: Computes the volume of a rectangular box (cuboid) by multiplying its length l, width w and height h. The result is in cubed units of the length unit used.
notes: All three dimensions must be in the same unit; the result is that unit cubed. Applies to a right rectangular box with mutually perpendicular edges.

name: Rectangular box surface area
description: Gives the total surface area of a rectangular box as twice the sum of the three distinct face areas: length times width, width times height, and height times length. The result is in squared length units.
notes: This assumes a closed box with all six faces. All three dimensions must share the same unit.

name: Box space diagonal
description: Calculates the length of the longest internal diagonal of a rectangular box as the square root of the sum of the squares of its length l, width w and height h. This is the straight-line distance between opposite corners. The result is in the same length unit.
notes: This is the three-dimensional Pythagorean theorem for the corner-to-corner diagonal, not a face diagonal. All three dimensions must share the same unit.

name: Pyramid volume
description: Computes the volume of any pyramid as its base area b times its height h, divided by three. It equals one third of a prism with the same base and height. The result is in cubed length units.
notes: The first input b is already the base area, not a base edge, and h is the perpendicular height from base to apex. The base-area unit and the height unit must be consistent.

name: Square pyramid volume
description: Gives the volume of a pyramid with a square base as the base edge a squared times the height h, divided by three. The result is in cubed units of the length unit used.
notes: The input a is the base edge length (the base area is a squared), and h is the perpendicular height to the apex, not the slant height. Edge and height must share the same unit.

name: Torus volume
description: Calculates the volume of a torus (doughnut shape) as two pi squared times the center radius R times the tube radius r squared. The result is in cubed units of the radii.
notes: R is the distance from the center of the hole to the center of the tube, and r is the tube's own radius; a proper ring requires R greater than r. Both radii must use the same unit.

name: Torus surface area
description: Computes the surface area of a torus as four pi squared times the center radius R times the tube radius r. The result is in squared units of the radii.
notes: R is the distance from the center to the middle of the tube, and r is the tube radius; a valid torus needs R greater than r. Both radii must share the same unit.

name: Regular tetrahedron volume
description: Gives the volume of a regular tetrahedron (a solid with four equal equilateral-triangle faces) from its edge length a, equal to a cubed divided by six times the square root of two. The result is in cubed units of the edge length.
notes: Valid only for a regular tetrahedron where all six edges are equal. The result unit is the edge unit cubed.

name: Spherical cap volume
description: Computes the volume of a spherical cap, the portion of a sphere cut off by a plane, as pi times the cap height h squared times (three times the sphere radius r minus h), divided by three. The result is in cubed length units.
notes: The cap height h is measured from the cutting plane to the top of the cap and must not exceed the sphere radius r for a cap (h equal to 2r would give the whole sphere).

name: Ellipsoid volume
description: Calculates the volume of an ellipsoid as four thirds of pi times the product of its three semi-axes a, b and c. When all three are equal it reduces to the volume of a sphere. The result is in cubed length units.
notes: Use the semi-axes (half-lengths along each axis), not the full axis lengths. All three must share the same unit.

name: Distance between two points (2D)
description: Computes the straight-line distance between two points in a plane, (x1, y1) and (x2, y2), as the hypotenuse of the differences in x and y. The result is a distance in the same unit as the coordinates.
notes: This is the Euclidean (straight-line) distance from the Pythagorean theorem; it is unchanged if the two points are swapped. All coordinates must use the same unit.

name: Distance between two points (3D)
description: Gives the straight-line distance between two points in space, (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2), as the square root of the sum of the squared differences of the three coordinates. The result is in the same unit as the coordinates.
notes: This extends the Pythagorean theorem to three dimensions and is symmetric in the two points. All six coordinates must use the same unit.

name: Slope of a line
description: Calculates the slope of a straight line through two points as the change in y divided by the change in x, that is (y2 minus y1) over (x2 minus x1). The result is a dimensionless rise-over-run ratio.
notes: The slope is undefined for a vertical line where x2 equals x1, since that divides by zero. A positive result rises left to right, a negative result falls.

name: Conical frustum volume
description: Computes the volume of a conical frustum (a cone with its top sliced off parallel to the base) as (1/3)*pi*h*(R^2 + R*r + r^2), using the bottom radius R, top radius r, and height h.
notes: R and r are the two circular radii and h is the perpendicular height between them, not the slant height. All lengths must share one unit; the volume comes out in that unit cubed.

name: Conical frustum lateral surface area
description: Computes the curved (lateral) surface area of a conical frustum as pi*(R+r)*sqrt((R-r)^2 + h^2), excluding the two circular ends. The square-root term is the slant height derived from the radius difference and vertical height.
notes: This covers only the side wall, not the top and bottom disks. h is the vertical height; the formula computes the slant height internally. Keep all lengths in the same unit.

name: Conical frustum total surface area
description: Computes the total surface area of a conical frustum, pi*(R^2 + r^2 + (R+r)*sqrt((R-r)^2 + h^2)), summing the two circular ends and the curved lateral surface.
notes: Includes both the top and bottom disks plus the side wall. h is the vertical height, not the slant height. Use a single consistent length unit for R, r, and h.

name: Spherical cap curved surface area
description: Computes the curved surface area of a spherical cap as 2*pi*r*h, where r is the radius of the full sphere and h is the height of the cap. This is the area of the dome-shaped part only.
notes: This gives only the curved (spherical) surface, excluding the flat circular base of the cap. h is the cap height measured along the sphere axis and must satisfy 0 <= h <= 2r.

name: Spherical cap base radius
description: Computes the radius of the flat circular base of a spherical cap as sqrt(h*(2r - h)), from the sphere radius r and cap height h. This is the radius of the circle where the cap meets the rest of the sphere.
notes: h is the cap height and must satisfy 0 <= h <= 2r so the term under the square root stays non-negative. The base radius is largest at h = r (a hemisphere) and returns to zero at h = 2r.

name: Spherical sector volume
description: Computes the volume of a spherical sector as (2/3)*pi*r^2*h, where r is the sphere radius and h is the cap height. A spherical sector is the solid swept from the sphere center out to a spherical cap.
notes: h is the height of the corresponding cap, with 0 <= h <= 2r. This is the cone-plus-cap solid bounded by the sphere center, not the spherical cap segment alone. Keep r and h in the same unit.

name: Paraboloid volume
description: Computes the volume of a solid paraboloid of revolution as (1/2)*pi*r^2*h, with base radius r and height h. Its volume is exactly half that of the enclosing cylinder of the same radius and height.
notes: Applies to a paraboloid formed by rotating a parabola about its axis, not to a cone or hemisphere. r is the radius at the flat circular base. Use consistent length units.

name: Regular tetrahedron surface area
description: Computes the total surface area of a regular tetrahedron as sqrt(3)*a^2, where a is the edge length. This sums the areas of its four identical equilateral-triangle faces.
notes: Valid only for a regular tetrahedron, whose four faces are congruent equilateral triangles. a is the edge length; the result is in that unit squared.

name: Regular tetrahedron height
description: Computes the height of a regular tetrahedron as a*sqrt(2/3), the perpendicular distance from one vertex to the opposite triangular face, given edge length a.
notes: This is the apex-to-base height of a regular tetrahedron, not the face height or edge length. Valid only when all edges are equal to a.

name: Regular octahedron volume
description: Computes the volume of a regular octahedron as (sqrt(2)/3)*a^3, where a is the edge length. A regular octahedron is the solid with eight equilateral-triangle faces, like two square pyramids joined at their bases.
notes: Valid only for a regular octahedron with all edges equal to a. The result is in that length unit cubed.

name: Regular octahedron surface area
description: Computes the total surface area of a regular octahedron as 2*sqrt(3)*a^2, where a is the edge length. This sums the areas of its eight identical equilateral-triangle faces.
notes: Valid only for a regular octahedron whose eight faces are congruent equilateral triangles. a is the edge length; the result is in that unit squared.

name: Regular dodecahedron volume
description: Computes the volume of a regular dodecahedron as ((15 + 7*sqrt(5))/4)*a^3, where a is the edge length. A regular dodecahedron is the solid bounded by twelve regular pentagonal faces.
notes: Valid only for a regular dodecahedron with all edges equal to a. The constant (15 + 7*sqrt(5))/4 is about 7.6631. The result is in that length unit cubed.

name: Regular dodecahedron surface area
description: Computes the total surface area of a regular dodecahedron as 3*sqrt(25 + 10*sqrt(5))*a^2, where a is the edge length. This sums the areas of its twelve regular pentagonal faces.
notes: Valid only for a regular dodecahedron with all edges equal to a. The coefficient 3*sqrt(25 + 10*sqrt(5)) is about 20.6457. The result is in that unit squared.

name: Regular icosahedron volume
description: Computes the volume of a regular icosahedron as (5/12)*(3 + sqrt(5))*a^3, where a is the edge length. A regular icosahedron is the solid bounded by twenty equilateral-triangle faces.
notes: Valid only for a regular icosahedron with all edges equal to a. The constant (5/12)*(3 + sqrt(5)) is about 2.1817. The result is in that length unit cubed.

name: Regular icosahedron surface area
description: Computes the total surface area of a regular icosahedron as 5*sqrt(3)*a^2, where a is the edge length. This sums the areas of its twenty identical equilateral-triangle faces.
notes: Valid only for a regular icosahedron whose twenty faces are congruent equilateral triangles. a is the edge length; the result is in that unit squared.

name: Regular hexagonal prism volume
description: Computes the volume of a regular hexagonal prism as (3*sqrt(3)/2)*a^2*h, the area of the regular-hexagon base (3*sqrt(3)/2)*a^2 multiplied by the prism height h. Here a is the base edge length.
notes: a is the side length of the regular hexagonal base, not a diagonal, and h is the prism height perpendicular to the base. Use consistent length units.

name: Regular hexagonal prism surface area
description: Computes the total surface area of a regular hexagonal prism as 3*sqrt(3)*a^2 + 6*a*h, combining the two hexagonal ends (3*sqrt(3)*a^2 total) with the six rectangular side faces (6*a*h). Here a is the base edge and h the height.
notes: a is the side length of the hexagonal base and h is the prism height. The first term covers both hexagonal ends; the second covers the six identical rectangular sides. Keep a and h in the same unit.

name: Square pyramid total surface area
description: Computes the total surface area of a right square pyramid as a^2 + 2*a*sqrt((a/2)^2 + h^2), adding the square base area a^2 to the four triangular sides. The square-root term is the slant height from the vertical height h.
notes: Applies to a right pyramid with a square base of side a and apex over the center. h is the vertical height, not the slant height, which the formula derives internally. Includes the base.

name: Regular polygon area from side
description: Computes the area of a regular n-sided polygon from its side length s as (n*s^2)/(4*tan(pi/n)). It multiplies the number of sides and squared side length, scaled by a factor set by the interior geometry.
notes: n must be an integer of 3 or more, and the angle pi/n is in radians. s is the length of one side. Valid only for regular (equilateral, equiangular) polygons.

name: Regular polygon apothem
description: Computes the apothem of a regular n-sided polygon as s/(2*tan(pi/n)), the perpendicular distance from the center to the midpoint of any side, given side length s.
notes: n must be an integer of 3 or more and pi/n is in radians. The apothem reaches to the middle of a side, not to a vertex (which is the circumradius). Valid for regular polygons only.

name: Regular polygon circumradius
description: Computes the circumradius of a regular n-sided polygon as s/(2*sin(pi/n)), the distance from the center to any vertex, given side length s. This is the radius of the circle passing through all vertices.
notes: n must be an integer of 3 or more and pi/n is in radians. The circumradius reaches a vertex, unlike the apothem, which reaches a side midpoint. Valid for regular polygons only.

name: Regular polygon interior angle (radians)
description: Computes the interior angle of a regular n-sided polygon as ((n-2)*pi)/n, in radians. This is the angle at each vertex between two adjacent sides.
notes: n must be an integer of 3 or more, and the result is in radians (multiply by 180/pi for degrees). It grows toward pi as n increases. All vertices share this angle in a regular polygon.

name: Regular hexagon area
description: Computes the area of a regular hexagon as (3*sqrt(3)/2)*a^2, where a is the side length. A regular hexagon equals six equilateral triangles of side a arranged around its center.
notes: Valid only for a regular hexagon with all sides equal to a. The coefficient 3*sqrt(3)/2 is about 2.598. The result is in that length unit squared.

name: Circular arc length
description: Computes the length of a circular arc as r*theta, the radius r multiplied by the central angle theta in radians. It gives the distance measured along the curved arc.
notes: theta must be in radians, not degrees; convert degrees by multiplying by pi/180. The result is a length in the same unit as r, not the straight-line chord.

name: Ellipse perimeter (Ramanujan approx.)
description: Estimates the perimeter of an ellipse with Ramanujan's approximation pi*(3*(a+b) - sqrt((3*a+b)*(a+3*b))), from the semi-major axis a and semi-minor axis b. It is highly accurate for most ellipses.
notes: a and b are the semi-axes (half the full axis lengths), not the full diameters. This is an approximation; error grows for very elongated ellipses but stays tiny for moderate ones.

name: Ellipse eccentricity
description: Computes the eccentricity of an ellipse as sqrt(1 - b^2/a^2), from the semi-major axis a and semi-minor axis b. The result, between 0 and 1, measures how elongated the ellipse is; 0 is a circle.
notes: a must be the larger (semi-major) axis and b the smaller (semi-minor) so the term under the root stays non-negative. Eccentricity is dimensionless and approaches 1 for very flat ellipses.

name: Cube space diagonal
description: Computes the space (body) diagonal of a cube as a*sqrt(3), where a is the edge length. This is the straight-line distance between two opposite corners passing through the cube interior.
notes: This is the internal corner-to-corner diagonal, not a face diagonal (a*sqrt(2)) or an edge. Valid only for a cube with all edges equal to a.

name: Rectangular box space diagonal
description: Computes the space diagonal of a rectangular box as sqrt(l^2 + w^2 + h^2), from its length l, width w, and height h. This is the straight-line distance between opposite corners through the box interior.
notes: This is the 3D corner-to-corner diagonal, a direct extension of the Pythagorean theorem, not a face diagonal. All three dimensions must use the same length unit.

name: Distance from point to line (2D)
description: Computes the perpendicular distance from a point (x, y) to the line a*x + b*y + c = 0 as abs(a*x + b*y + c)/sqrt(a^2 + b^2). It gives the shortest straight-line distance from the point to the line.
notes: The line must be given in general form a*x + b*y + c = 0; a and b cannot both be zero. The absolute value makes the distance non-negative regardless of which side the point lies on.

name: Distance from point to plane (3D)
expression: abs(a*x + b*y + c*z + d)/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2)
description: Computes the perpendicular distance from a point (x, y, z) to the plane a*x + b*y + c*z + d = 0 as abs(a*x + b*y + c*z + d)/sqrt(a^2 + b^2 + c^2). It gives the shortest distance from the point to the plane.
notes: The plane must be in general form a*x + b*y + c*z + d = 0, where (a, b, c) is its normal vector and cannot be all zero. The absolute value keeps the distance non-negative.

name: Triangle area from coordinates (shoelace)
description: Computes the area of a triangle from its three vertex coordinates using the shoelace formula abs(x1*(y2-y3) + x2*(y3-y1) + x3*(y1-y2))/2. It works directly from the corner points without needing side lengths.
notes: Vertices may be given in any order; the absolute value ensures a non-negative area. If the three points are collinear the area is zero. All coordinates should share the same unit.

name: Vector magnitude (3D)
description: Computes the magnitude (length) of a 3D vector as sqrt(x^2 + y^2 + z^2), from its three components. This is the Euclidean distance from the origin to the point (x, y, z).
notes: x, y, and z are the vector components along each axis. The result is always non-negative and shares the components' unit. This is the 3D form of the Pythagorean theorem.

name: Dot product (3D)
description: Computes the dot (scalar) product of two 3D vectors as x1*x2 + y1*y2 + z1*z2. The result is a single number that reflects how aligned the two vectors are, positive when they point in similar directions.
notes: The result is a scalar, not a vector. It is zero when the two vectors are perpendicular and equals the product of magnitudes times the cosine of the angle between them.

name: Angle between two vectors (2D)
description: Computes the angle between two 2D vectors as acos((x1*x2 + y1*y2)/(sqrt(x1^2 + y1^2)*sqrt(x2^2 + y2^2))), using the dot product divided by the product of magnitudes. The result is in radians.
notes: Neither vector may have zero length, or the division is undefined. The result is in radians between 0 and pi; multiply by 180/pi for degrees. It gives the unsigned angle.

name: Angle between two vectors (3D)
description: Computes the angle between two 3D vectors as acos((x1*x2 + y1*y2 + z1*z2)/(sqrt(x1^2 + y1^2 + z1^2)*sqrt(x2^2 + y2^2 + z2^2))), the dot product divided by the product of magnitudes. The result is in radians.
notes: Neither vector may have zero length. The result is in radians between 0 and pi (multiply by 180/pi for degrees) and is the unsigned angle, independent of vector order.

name: Cross product magnitude (2D)
description: Computes the magnitude of the 2D cross product as abs(x1*y2 - x2*y1). This scalar equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors, or twice the area of the triangle they form.
notes: In 2D the cross product is a scalar; the absolute value discards its sign (orientation). It is zero when the two vectors are parallel or collinear.

name: Cross product magnitude (3D)
description: Computes the magnitude of the 3D cross product as sqrt((y1*z2 - z1*y2)^2 + (z1*x2 - x1*z2)^2 + (x1*y2 - y1*x2)^2). This equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors.
notes: This gives only the length of the cross-product vector, not its direction. It is zero when the two vectors are parallel and maximal when they are perpendicular.

name: Hemisphere Volume
description: Calculates the volume enclosed by a hemisphere (half of a sphere) of radius r, using (2/3)×π×r³ — exactly half the volume of a full sphere of the same radius.
notes: r is the radius, not the diameter. This is half of the full-sphere formula (4/3)πr³, since a hemisphere is exactly half a sphere.

name: Hemisphere Surface Area (Total)
description: Computes the total surface area of a solid hemisphere, combining the curved (domed) surface 2πr² with the flat circular base πr², for a total of 3πr².
notes: For only the curved surface without the base, use 2πr² instead. r is the radius, not the diameter.

name: Circular Sector Perimeter
description: Computes the perimeter of a circular sector (pie slice) as the arc length plus the two straight radii, given radius r and central angle θ.
notes: θ is entered in degrees and converted internally to radians for the arc-length term r×θ. Keep θ between 0° and 360° for a physically meaningful sector.

name: Triangle Circumradius
description: Finds the radius R of the circumscribed circle (the circle passing through all three vertices) of a triangle from its three side lengths a, b, c, using R = abc/(4×Area) with the triangle's area computed inline via Heron's formula.
notes: a, b, c must satisfy the triangle inequality (each side shorter than the sum of the other two), otherwise the square root becomes undefined.

name: Triangle Inradius
description: Finds the radius r of the inscribed circle (the largest circle fitting inside a triangle, tangent to all three sides) from its side lengths a, b, c, using r = Area/s where s is the semiperimeter and Area is computed inline via Heron's formula.
notes: a, b, c must satisfy the triangle inequality. s = (a+b+c)/2 is the semiperimeter, computed inline rather than as a separate variable.
